questions.q: Three entry points (an HTTP route, a CLI tool, a batch job) each run their own copy of the authentication, authorization and validation checks. What is the main risk?
questions.explain: Every copy compiles and passes its own tests. The bug is the line nobody wrote a second time. One pipeline shared by every entry point removes the copies.
options: One copy silently misses a check, and nothing fails until someone abuses that entry point
The checks run in parallel and race each other

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first middleware starts first and finishes last, and it can change the result on the way out: a upper-cased what the handler returned.
options: PAID a in, b in, handler, a out
paid a in, b in, handler, a out
PAID b in, a in, handler, a out
PAID a in, a out, b in, handler

questions.q: What does createPipeline's function return when a middleware throws, with the default options?
questions.explain: The default error mode is "capture": the chain stops and the failure is reported in the outcome, including executedMiddleware and errors.
options: An outcome with success: false, the error, and the names of the middleware that started
An outcome with success: true and result: undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: executedMiddleware lists the middleware that started, so the failing authenticate is included and validate never ran. The failure is recorded once in errors.

questions.q: Why can you write if (outcome.success) use(outcome.result) without TypeScript complaining that result may be undefined?
questions.explain: PipelineResult is PipelineSuccess | PipelineFailure, told apart by success: true or false. Narrowing on it is the TypeScript pattern from the unions lesson.
options: The outcome is a discriminated union on success, so checking it narrows to the success type with a non-optional result

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Lower priority runs first, the default is 100, disabled middleware is dropped, and equal priorities keep their list order. That last rule put authorize before authenticate: a real bug in a security chain.

questions.q: What priority does a named middleware get when you give none?
questions.explain: The default is 100 and lower numbers run earlier. errorMiddleware uses 0, so it runs before everything with the default.

questions.q: When one file builds the whole pipeline, why does this lesson prefer a plain list in the right order over priorities?
questions.explain: Priorities help when middleware comes from several places. Within one file, the list itself is the clearest statement of order.
options: The order can be read directly from the list, and ties between equal priorities cannot silently reorder security checks

questions.q: In the transfer context, token and body are readonly while user and transfer are optional and writable. Why?
questions.explain: Only authenticate sets user and only validate sets transfer. A handler that reads them knows they were checked; a handler reading body would skip validation.
options: Readonly fields are faster to read
The transport fields are what the caller sent and must not be rewritten; the trusted fields are filled in by the middleware that checked them
Optional fields are not sent over HTTP
TypeScript requires context objects to have optional fields

questions.q: Which value should the transfer handler use for the amount?
questions.explain: The raw body is untrusted: it may be missing, a string or negative. The parsed transfer exists only if validation passed, which is the whole point of putting validation before the handler.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: capture stops and reports. continue records the failure, skips the rest of that middleware and still runs the handler, so the outcome succeeds with one recorded error.
options:
capture false - 1
continue true transfer done 1

capture true transfer done 1
continue true transfer done 0

capture false - 0
continue true transfer done 0

questions.q: Why must a pipeline that contains authenticate never use errorMode: "continue"?
questions.explain: continue is for truly optional steps such as an audit log. For a security check, "skip the failing middleware and carry on" means "let the attacker in".
options: A thrown authentication failure would be recorded and skipped, and the request would still reach the handler
Because authentication errors cannot be recorded

questions.q: When is errorMode: "throw" the right choice?
questions.explain: "throw" stops the chain and lets the error propagate. The deprecated option is stopOnError, not errorMode.
options: For HTTP routes, so errors become 500
When the caller already has its own try/catch that decides what to do, such as a job runner deciding whether to retry
When you want the pipeline to continue after an error

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A second next() would run the handler, and the payment, twice. The pipeline refuses it before the handler runs again. A retry belongs inside the handler, around the operation you know is safe to repeat.

questions.q: What does errorMiddleware(onError) do with an error thrown further down the pipeline?
questions.explain: It is a reporter, not a handler. With priority 0 it runs first, so it sees every error of the middleware after it.
options: Calls onError with it and rethrows it, so the pipeline's error mode still decides the outcome
Retries the rest of the pipeline once

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The timeout made the pipeline stop waiting, but the work it was waiting for kept running and finished later. A timeout means "I don't know", never "it did not happen".

questions.q: A payment call must really stop when the timeout fires. What do you need?
questions.explain: Nothing in the middleware contract can stop a promise that is already running. Only code that checks a signal can stop, which is why fetch and many clients accept one.
options: Two timeout middleware in a row
An AbortSignal that the payment call itself checks, passed through the context

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pipeline checks its signal before each middleware and before the handler. An aborted signal fails the run with MiddlewareAbortedError without calling the handler.

questions.q: A request path is /transfers\n[INFO] admin logged in. Why does loggingMiddleware write the newline as the two characters \n?
questions.explain: Escaping control characters keeps every caller-supplied value inside its own line, while the original stays readable. sanitizeLogValue does the same for your own lines.
options: So the caller cannot forge a second, real-looking log line (log injection)
Because log files cannot contain newlines
To hide the path from the log

questions.q: Why does loggingMiddleware leave the error message out of its completion line by default?
questions.explain: A message like connection to postgres://bank:s3cret@db failed would put a password in the logs. Opt in with includeErrorMessage: true only when your messages are safe.
options: Error messages often contain connection strings, tokens or user data; the error object still reaches the caller
Because errors are logged by the runtime instead

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Control characters are escaped, not dropped, so the value stays visible without breaking out of its line. The second argument truncates long values and marks the cut with an ellipsis.

questions.q: Where does rateLimitMiddleware find the key it counts by?
questions.explain: It reads context.key. In the transfer pipeline, authenticate sets it to the user id, so each user has their own allowance.
options: It counts all requests together, always

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every request without a key lands in one shared bucket with an allowance of two, so the third unkeyed request is refused, while ada has her own bucket. rejectUnkeyed: true refuses unkeyed requests instead of pooling them.

questions.q: What goes wrong if the per-user rate limiter runs before authenticate?
questions.explain: The limiter can only count per user once the user is known. With rejectUnkeyed: true the wrong order fails loudly instead of quietly pooling everyone.
options: Nothing; order does not matter for rate limits
context.key is not set yet, so every request shares one bucket and one noisy client can lock everybody out
The limiter counts each request twice
Authentication errors are no longer reported

questions.q: A MiddlewareRateLimitError is thrown out of a route in @zudojs/http. What does the client get in the published packages?
questions.explain: The error carries retryAfterMs, but not an HTTP status the server honours. The adapter in this lesson checks instanceof MiddlewareRateLimitError and answers 429 with Retry-After.
options: A generic 500, because the error has status 500 and is not exposed; you must map it to 429 yourself

questions.q: The lesson puts validation before the rate limit. What is the benefit, and what is the cost?
questions.explain: A client with a bug gets a clear 400 instead of a 429. The expensive handler is still protected, and the HTTP pipeline's per-IP limiter stops floods of junk.
options: Benefit: malformed requests do not use up the caller's allowance. Cost: malformed requests are not limited by this step, so a per-IP limit in front is still needed
Benefit: the limiter can read the parsed body. Cost: validation runs twice
Benefit: none; it is only a convention

questions.q: Why does authorization run before validation in the transfer pipeline?
questions.explain: Refusing early leaks less and costs less. Validation error messages describe your input format, which an unauthorised caller does not need to see.
options: Validation needs to know the user's role
A caller who is not allowed to transfer learns nothing about what a valid transfer looks like, and no work is spent validating a request that will be refused

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: @zudojs/http recognises a guard response by its brand and sends it with its own status and body. This lets a guard written without importing @zudojs/http refuse requests.

questions.q: Why is a guard response branded with a symbol instead of being any object with a status field?
questions.explain: A middleware may legitimately return data that happens to have a status key. Only the brand, which request data cannot forge, turns an object into a response.
options: JSON cannot carry a symbol, so data from a request can never be mistaken for a response
So it can be serialised to JSON

questions.q: In the transfer example, which part knows about HTTP status codes?
questions.explain: Keeping the pipeline transport-independent is what lets a CLI tool or a queue job run it too. The errors carry meaning (401, 403, 400); only the adapter decides how to present them.
options: Only the route adapter that turns the pipeline outcome into a response

questions.q: The Task API registers the import pipeline in the container as a singleton. What would go wrong if it created a new pipeline for every request?
questions.explain: The limiter's counts live inside the middleware instance. One shared pipeline means one shared set of counts for all requests in the process.
options: The pipeline would be garbage collected too early
Each request would get a fresh rate limiter, so the limit would never be reached

questions.q: Why does the import pipeline compare SHA-256 digests with timingSafeEqual instead of token === expected?
questions.explain: === can stop at the first different character, which leaks timing. Equal-length digests compared in constant time avoid that, and storing only digests means a leaked configuration does not reveal tokens.
options: The comparison takes the same time however many characters match, and the server never stores the raw token
Because === does not work on strings from headers

questions.q: Write your own compose(middleware, handler): it returns a function of a context that runs the middleware in order around the handler, and throws Error("next() called twice") if a middleware calls next more than once.
questions.explain: Each middleware gets a next that dispatches the one after it; the last next calls the handler. A flag per middleware refuses a second call, which is exactly what @zudojs/middleware does with MiddlewareNextCalledMultipleTimesError.
questions.expected:
paid auth in > validate in > handler > validate out > auth out
next() called twice

questions.q: Write createLimiter(max, windowMs) with a method allow(key, now) that implements a sliding window: keep each key's timestamps, forget those older than windowMs, allow when fewer than max remain. Time is passed in, so the test is deterministic.
questions.explain: At 59 seconds Ada still has two requests in the last minute, so she is refused; at 61 seconds the one from second 0 has left the window. A fixed window reset at 60 seconds would have let her send four requests in two seconds around the boundary.

questions.q: The pipeline below is in the wrong order: the limiter runs before authentication, so every request shares one bucket. Reorder the list so the output shows Ada refused on her third request while Bayo is still allowed.
questions.explain: In the starter order, all four requests share the (shared) bucket, so Bayo is refused because of Ada. After authentication has set the key, each user has an own allowance.

questions.q: Write toStatus(error) for a pipeline adapter: an object with retryAfterMs gives "429 retry-after=N" (seconds, rounded up); an object with expose: true and a numeric statusCode below 500 gives that status; anything else gives "500".
questions.explain: Only errors that are explicitly marked safe to show become client errors. Everything else is a 500 with no details, and the rate-limit error is mapped deliberately because it does not carry a 429 of its own.

questions.q: Write a middleware-like function dailyCap(capKobo) that returns (userId, amountKobo, next). It refuses (returns "refused") when the user's total plus this amount would exceed the cap, otherwise calls next() and adds the amount only if next() returned "ok".
questions.explain: Counting only after the rest of the pipeline succeeded means a failed transfer does not eat into the cap: Ada's second attempt failed, so her third went through and only the fourth hit the ₦100,000 limit.
questions.expected: ok, insufficient funds, ok, refused, ok

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each user id is its own key with an allowance of one per minute. Bayo is unaffected by Ada; Ada's second request is limited.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a write function, loggingMiddleware writes nothing; it never falls back to the console. It still runs, so it appears in executedMiddleware.
options: An error: a logger is required

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: errorMiddleware has priority 0, lower than any other here, so it is placed first and wraps everything after it. authenticate (10) comes before validate (default 100).
